I have tried to practice the art of noticing. Not the grand, cinematic moments, but the small textures of ordinary life: the way light slants through a window at 4 p.m., the particular squeak of the third step on the staircase, the quiet sigh a kettle makes before it boils. These details do not ask for attention, yet they hold the world together.

As a child, I noticed everything—the shapes in ceiling cracks, the smell of rain on hot pavement, the exact weight of a library book. Somewhere along the way, that attention faded. To be an adult is often to move through days with a kind of efficient blindness, checking tasks off lists, walking past trees without seeing them. Relearning noticing has felt like waking up a muscle that had gone stiff.

Yesterday I sat on a bench and watched a pigeon. Not a remarkable bird, but its movements were precise and full of tiny decisions. It tilted its head at a crumb, stepped sideways, assessed me with one orange eye. For two minutes, I was completely absorbed. There was no urgency, no scrolling, no inner monologue about productivity. Just a pigeon and me, sharing a patch of sidewalk.

I think this is a form of freedom. The world offers an infinite number of small doors, and attention is the key. You need not travel far or buy anything. You need to slow down enough to let the ordinary become visible again. That seems a reasonable way to live.
